OrthoEraser: Coupled-Neuron Orthogonal Projection for Concept Erasure

Erase a sensitive concept while explicitly protecting the benign features coupled to the intervention.

Shi Chuancheng · Wu Wenhua · Shen Fei · Zhu Xiaogang · Hu Kun · Wang Zhiyong

March 12, 2026 ·ECCV 2026 ·Read the paper ·PDF
1Why this matters 2How it works 3What the study finds 4What this means

The short version

OrthoEraser studies concept erasure through the geometry of entangled features. It locates sensitive neurons and identifies coupled features whose responses overlap with the target. An orthogonal projection constrains the intervention relative to the coupled benign subspace, aiming to suppress the target while reducing collateral changes.

The evaluation pairs removal effectiveness with generation fidelity and feature-level analysis. This makes selectivity a first-class objective: a stronger intervention is useful when its behavioral effect is specific enough to preserve legitimate generation.

SAESparse feature decomposition
NullConstrained erasure projection
CoupledBenign features to protect

Precise concept removal requires understanding what the target shares with the capabilities we want to preserve.

Why this matters

Suppressing a whole unit can also remove benign attributes because sensitive and benign semantics need not occupy orthogonal activation spaces.

How it works

  1. Decompose dense activations with an SAE and identify sensitive units.
  2. Detect coupled benign units that are vulnerable to the proposed intervention.
  3. Project erasure vectors into the coupled units’ null space using analytical orthogonalization.

What the study finds

The paper evaluates erasure precision and preservation of non-sensitive generation together. Reported comparisons support the benefit of explicitly protecting the identified benign subspace.

What this means

Controllability depends on the resolution of an intervention. When harmful and benign features share directions, indiscriminate suppression can damage both. Geometry provides a way to express which components should change and which should be protected.

The broader lesson is to evaluate editing through a joint account of suppression and preservation. The tested projection offers evidence for a more selective mechanism; its guarantees are limited to the modeled subspace and experimental settings, motivating continued checks for residual behavior and side effects.
